sentences.text: The genus Vegasaurus contains only one known species, Vegasaurus molyi.
This animal is unique among elasmosaurids for having fifty-four neck vertebrae.
Scientists estimate its body length was between six point one five and six point five meters, with a mass of eight hundred thirty-nine kilograms.
The species is known only from the holotype specimen MLP 93-I-5-1, a nearly complete postcranial skeleton missing the tail tip, housed at the La Plata Museum in Argentina.
Eduardo Olivero, Daniel Martinioni, Francisco Mussel, and Jorge Lusky found the fossil in 1989 at Cape Lamb on Vega Island, the northernmost part of the Antarctic Peninsula.
José P. O'Gorman, Leonardo Salgado, Eduardo B. Olivero, and Sergio A. Marenssi first described and named the creature in 2015.
Evidence of a past injury appears as a pathological bone callus on a rib, indicating the animal healed from a fracture.
The skeleton includes the entire neck, various back and tail vertebrae, girdles, limbs, ribs, and forty-five gastroliths found near the dorsal region.
Phylogenetic analysis places Vegasaurus with Morenosaurus and the aristonectines Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea, all Late Cretaceous South Pacific elasmosaurids.
Vegasaurus differs from Aristonectinae by having elongated neck vertebrae, linking it to taxa like Futabasaurus from the other side of the Pacific.
Vegasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from seventy-two point two to sixty-six million years ago.
